overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Long History of Bathing on Shabbat
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 40a–40b
overview.hebrewSource: בַּתְּחִילָּה הָיוּ רוֹחֲצִין בְּחַמִּין שֶׁהוּחַמּוּ מֵעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Having established that hot water heated before Shabbat may sometimes be used afterward, the Gemara asks exactly how much washing that permits — the whole body or just exposed limbs? A closely-argued dispute between Rav and Shmuel is settled against Rav, and the Gemara then tells the remarkable history of how bathhouse customs in Tiberias were tightened again and again as people exploited each new leniency. The daf closes with the boundary between merely warming an object (water, oil, a towel) and actually cooking it — including oil's own uncertain status — illustrated by a story of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi teaching halakha from inside the bathhouse itself.

slides.title: 📈 The Escalating History of Tiberias Bathing Decrees
slides.subtitle: Each new leniency was exploited, prompting a stricter one

steps.content: 1️⃣ Originally: people bathed in hot water heated before Shabbat — permitted
2️⃣ Bathhouse attendants began secretly heating water on Shabbat, claiming it was pre-heated → Sages banned hot bathing, permitted only sweating
3️⃣ People kept bathing in hot water, claiming 'we are only sweating' → Sages banned sweating too, but permitted the natural hot springs of Tiberias
4️⃣ People bathed in ordinary fire-heated water, falsely claiming it was spring water → Sages banned even the Tiberias springs, permitting only cold water
5️⃣ The public could not sustain such strictness, so the Sages restored permission for the Tiberias springs — while the ban on sweating in a heated bathhouse remained

slides.title: 🫒 Is Oil Subject to the Prohibition of Cooking?
slides.subtitle: The first tanna's silent position, reconstructed two opposite ways

lines.speaker: Rabba & R. Yosef
lines.text: The first tanna holds oil is not subject to cooking at all — it may be warmed even to the point where a hand would recoil from it.

lines.speaker: R. Nachman b.Y.
lines.text: No — the first tanna holds oil is subject to cooking, and forbids warming it even below that threshold.

lines.speaker: Rav Yehuda
lines.text: In Shmuel's name, resolving the matter for both oil and water: heating to the point a hand recoils is forbidden; below that point, permitted.

lines.speaker: Rachava
lines.text: And the measure of 'a hand recoils' is: any heat that would scald a baby's stomach.

slides.title: 🛁 Three Lessons From a Bathhouse Instruction
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi teaches halakha without saying a word of Torah
slides.label: The incident:
slides.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi wanted to place a jar of oil directly into Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's bathtub to warm it. Rabbi told him instead: 'Take water in a second vessel and pour the oil in there.' The Gemara draws three halakhot from this single instruction: that oil is subject to the prohibition of cooking (or he wouldn't have objected), that a second vessel does not cook (so pouring the oil there was safe), and that warming oil to lukewarm counts as cooking it. Though Torah matters are normally not to be spoken in a bathhouse, this was permitted because Rabbi was preventing a transgression — just as a story about a student of Rabbi Meir shows the same principle applied elsewhere.

summary.principle: The line between permitted warming and forbidden cooking runs through everything from bathwater to oil to a mother's hand — and history shows the Sages tightened Shabbat bathing rules again and again whenever people stretched each leniency past its intended limit.

flowSteps.content: 🚿 Rav's limb-by-limb whole-body washing is refuted; only face, hands, and feet are permitted
📈 Tiberias bathing customs were restricted in stages as each leniency was exploited
🔥 Tempering water or oil near a fire is fine; reversing the order or direct contact risks real cooking

columns.content: 🫒 Oil's status is disputed, resolved by the universal 'hand recoils' standard
🛁 Rabbi's second-vessel instruction teaches three halakhot at once

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: heating anything to the point a hand would recoil from it crosses into forbidden cooking

quiz.q: What is the final halakhic outcome of the dispute between Rav and Shmuel about washing with water heated before Shabbat?
o: Rav's view is accepted: the whole body may be washed, one limb at a time
Shmuel's view stands: only the face, hands, and feet may be washed
Both views are rejected entirely
The dispute remains completely unresolved
quiz.e: A baraita explicitly refutes Rav's limb-by-limb leniency, leaving Shmuel's more restrictive position — face, hands, and feet only — in place.

quiz.q: According to the historical account traced to bar Kappara, why did the Sages eventually ban sweating in a heated bathhouse on Shabbat?
o: Sweating was always forbidden from the start
People who claimed to be 'only sweating' were actually bathing in forbidden hot water
Sweating was considered a form of theft
The bathhouses were closed for renovation
quiz.e: Each leniency was exploited by people falsely claiming to be doing the permitted thing, prompting the Sages to restrict it further and permit an alternative instead.

quiz.q: Why is it forbidden to rinse in cold water and then warm oneself by a bonfire, but permitted to do the reverse?
o: Fire may only be approached in the morning
Doing it in that order would heat the residual water on the body, a form of cooking
Cold water is always forbidden on Shabbat
There is no actual difference between the two orders
quiz.e: Warming by the fire first and rinsing after causes no cooking; reversing the order heats the water clinging to the body, which is prohibited.

quiz.q: What is the practical dispute between Rabba/Rav Yosef and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak regarding oil?
o: Whether oil may be eaten on Shabbat at all
Whether the first tanna considers oil subject to the prohibition of cooking
Whether oil can be used for Shabbat candles
Whether oil should be stored in glass or clay vessels
quiz.e: Rabba and Rav Yosef read the first tanna as permitting oil to be heated freely (not subject to cooking); Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reads him as forbidding it, since oil is subject to cooking.

quiz.q: What three halakhot does the Gemara derive from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi telling his student to pour oil into a second vessel of bath water?
o: That bathhouses must have two rooms, that oil floats, and that water must be changed daily
That oil is subject to cooking, that a second vessel does not cook, and that warming oil to lukewarm counts as cooking it
That Torah may never be discussed in a bathhouse under any circumstances
That only the Nasi may bathe with oil
quiz.e: All three halakhot are drawn from this single careful instruction, which also illustrates that preventing a transgression justifies speaking of such matters even in the bathhouse.
